extracted.intended_audience: science communicators and institutional press officers (universities, research institutes, government agencies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing science press releases that move beyond the deficit model toward two-way public engagement, emphasizing trust-building, plain-language ethics, and acknowledgement of public values and concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-deficit framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release avoid the implicit message 'if only the public understood X, they would support Y'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases written from the deficit posture trigger reader rejection on contested topics; avoid top-down lecturing that assumes public ignorance as the reason for disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-values acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release acknowledge — not dismiss — the values, concerns, and prior beliefs of the target public (religious, cultural, economic)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly name and respect the audiences' values and prior beliefs instead of treating them as obstacles to be corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidirectional posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release indicate that the issuing institution is learning from public input, not only teaching?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal willingness to adapt research priorities or communication in response to public feedback; present engagement as a two-way process rather than a one-way dissemination of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust-deficit recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release anticipate and address the public's lack of trust in scientists and institutions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borchelt-Hudson cite a 2004 survey finding ~40% of US residents do not trust scientists 'to put society's interest above their personal goals.' Releases should not assume institutional credibility and should proactively address trust concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of researcher motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release disclose the researcher's professional and financial stakes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openly stating potential conflicts or interests can defuse suspicion and reduce the trust-deficit; include relevant funding, affiliations, or personal stakes where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment of past failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release acknowledge prior instances where science has over-promised or failed (e.g., gene-therapy hype, neuroimaging overreach)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitting historical limits or past overstatements builds credibility and avoids the appearance of evasiveness or hubris.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain-language ethical frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release use plain language about ethical issues on ethically charged topics (genetics, AI, embryos) rather than technical hedging?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid evasive technical terminology when discussing ethics; make the ethical stakes clear in everyday language to avoid appearing dismissive of concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-input invitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release indicate channels for public comment, deliberation, or feedback rather than treating publication as a one-way broadcast?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, provide concrete mechanisms (forums, public meetings, comment portals) and encourage participation to demonstrate genuine engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trusted-translator availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release name and supply contact for community-trusted translators (clergy, patient-advocate groups, community physicians) when possible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide contacts beyond institutional spokespeople—trusted intermediaries can improve uptake and understanding among particular communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world consequence framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release frame the finding's practical implication for ordinary readers' lives rather than for the scientific community's internal status?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize everyday impacts and relevance to readers' concerns instead of focusing solely on novelty, metrics, or professional prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of jargon-as-authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release avoid using technical vocabulary as an authority signal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using jargon to impress can reinforce the deficit-model dynamic and reduce trust; favor clear explanations over technical name-dropping that distances readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release disclose research process details (who was involved, how decisions were made, what alternatives were considered)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about methods, decision points, and the limits of the work; this helps audiences evaluate credibility and reduces perceptions of hidden agendas.
